This report provides a summary of the pilot project involving the retrofit of two city of sask to heavy duty tracks with enhanced visibility and collision prediction systems.
The city's heavy duty tracks and equipment are not currently equipped with pedestrian or cyclist proximity detection and warning systems.
The goal of the pilot project was to assess two different types of systems as potential options for enhanced visibility for heavy duty tracks.
The building has selected a waste collection and the national patching track for the pilot project.
These trucks often work in areas where pedestrians and cyclists are present.
The pilot project included the installation of a 360 degree camera system and a collision prediction system in the waste collection track.
And the installation of a 360 degree artificial intelligence enhanced camera system in the actual patching track.
The systems were tested throughout the 2022 summer and 2025 winter maintenance seasons.
Feedback from the city operators that tested the piloted systems was used to assess their effectiveness.
The operators were surveyed using a questionnaire shared by transport candidate.
The overall assessment of the pilot project was that the systems were generally well accepted by the operators.
Five Canadian municipalities were contacted to understand current use of collision avoidance systems on their fleet vehicles.
Waste collection tracks have been commonly used for testing consistent with the city's pilot project.
The results of the jury's additional survey are summarized in the report.
Emerging AI technologies are developing and becoming increasingly accessible, including pedestrian and cyclist sensing and collision avoidance safety features on modern vehicles.

Currently, this technology is more advanced for light vehicles, but equipment manufacturers indicate optional original equipment manufacturer add-ons will become available for vocational tracks starting in 2026.
Information about the city's pilot project Bosch shared at the active transportation advisor group meeting in January 2025.

The two piloted systems have been purchased by the city at a total cost of $25,000.

Continue to use and assess that the two blind spot monitoring and detecting slash warning systems purchased by the city.

This report provides an update in the completion of an asset management plan and the long-term strategy for the management of the city of Saskatoon's corporate fuel and fueling infrastructure.

Historically, the management of fueling infrastructure in the city has been decentralized with the infrastructure oversight, maintenance and servicing being completed by the infrastructure user groups.
On a reactive basis.
Undefined was asset ownership resulted in an inconsistent approach to asset management, maintenance and operation of the fueling infrastructure throughout the organization.
In August 2020, the administration initiated a corporate fuel management project.

The objective of the project was to evaluate the current state of the fueling infrastructure and fuel management and develop an appropriate plan to address all the efficiencies and replace fueling infrastructure that has exceeded its design and service life.
Over the last five years, the administration has replaced the highest priority outdated underground fuel tanks with new above ground fuel tanks in the cities downtown yards.
The administration helps also completed infrastructure control, environmental, regulatory and safety improvements at 12 other fueling sites identified as a short-term priorities.

Additionally, capital funding was approved by city council as part of the 2025 multi-year business planning budget for the development of a corporate asset management plan and a long-term management strategy,
as well as the replacement of the next highest priority outdated underground fuel tanks.
In 2024, an analysis was completed to determine which city group was best positioned to take the ownership of the corporate fueling entry in assets.
The analysis identified the fleet service section in the roadways fleet and support department as the recommended asset owner.
In March 2025, a corporate fuel asset management plan was developed by a consultant.
The plan indicates that approximately $2.5 million is required for fueling infrastructure due for replacement over the next five years.
This funding request has been included in the 2026-27 major capital project prioritization list.
In May 2025, a long-term corporate fuel and fueling infrastructure management strategy was developed and approved by the city's senior leadership teams.
The long-term strategy includes replacement of outdated underground fuel tanks with above ground mobile fuel tanks.
In July 2025, an environmental site assessment began at the big-grandpole yards and Saskatoon lighting power sites.
The next highest priority sites for replacement of outdated underground fuel tanks.
The removal and replacement of the underground tanks at these locations is anticipated to be completed during the 2026 construction season.

In addition to the required capital funding, the fuel asset management plan has also identified annual operating funding required for the maintenance and management of the fueling infrastructure to maintain compliance within the standards and regulatory requirements.
The required operating funding is included in the administrative administrations in Ticative, 2026-27 multi-year business plan and budget.

The administration will decommission and replace existing fueling infrastructure in alignment with the fuel asset management plan and long-term corporate fuel and fueling infrastructure management strategy has allocated budget allows.
